title: Johnny:
headline: He came out of prison with nothing. Peer support changed his life. His one rule now: “We don't give advice.”
story: Ask Johnny what people get wrong about peer support. One word: advice. “We don't give advice. Let people be people.” People make their own mistakes and have their own victories.

He came out of prison with nothing, ran into peer support, and it changed everything. He has been at MHA for ten and a half years. It must feel warm, plain and a little funny, never like a counselor talking.

transcript:
Auto-transcript of 20260909_C4584.MP4 (Johnny, MHA office, Lincoln, 9 Sep 2026). Times are mm:ss in the source file. The transcript labels every line "Johnny", also the questions. Questions are marked (Interviewer) here.
[00:00] (Interviewer) name and your position here at MHA?
[00:03] My name is Johnny. I'm a peer support specialist at both of our houses.
[00:10] (Interviewer) Yeah, basically. How did you first come across MHA?
[00:15] Well, I took peer support training through the VA and then I knew a veteran that was working at MHA and yeah and then I volunteered and then I got hired on.
[00:27] (Interviewer) How long have you been here?
[00:29] Ten and a half years.
[00:30] (Interviewer) Awesome. What do you think makes peer support different than traditional support?
[00:35] The humanity. Yeah, I mean allowing people to be themselves and to chart their path instead of somebody else doing it for them and yeah.
[00:47] (Interviewer) Is there any moments that you still think about from experiences that you've had with participants through peer support?
[00:54] Oh yeah, all the time. All the time. I just messaged somebody in California that I know from the warm line.
[01:02] (Do not use 01:02–01:07: it points at a person who is inside right now.)
[01:07] The MHA is a... and I talk to people in Hawaii and New York from people that I've met on the warm line.
[01:13] (Crew talk, 01:13–01:34.)
[01:35] (Interviewer) So what would you say to somebody who doesn't believe that they can recover?
[01:43] Well, first of all, it's a hard position to be in because I was kind of there, you know what I mean, and I just try to instill some hope, you know what I mean, that things can change. I mean, I could use my story, but everybody's story is different, you know, and so hopefully my story would give some sort of hope, you know.
[02:01] (Interviewer) What do you think people get wrong about this work?
[02:10] Advice. Giving advice. We don't give advice. Let people be people. Let them make their own mistakes. Let them have their own victories. Yeah, so it's all them, yeah.
[02:22] (Interviewer) If someone watching has never heard of MHA, what should they know?
[02:29] Well, so I don't know, kind of, I look at it as kind of a ragtag bunch, you know what I mean, but we're super motivated and we will go to the wall for people. So I think it's, yeah, I think that's it. You're just kind of loose, but we're very serious in a way too, yeah.
[02:49] (Interviewer) Anything else you would like to add or any stories you would like to tell?
[02:58] I don't know. It's changed my life. Peer support has changed my life, and just real quick, I came out of prison. My life was nothing after 53 years, and I just decided I wanted to make something out of my life, and I ran into peer support, and it's changed everything in my life, you know what I mean. I never knew how much, how important it was to have people in your life, you know, people in your corner, and I took in school before way back, and I always wanted to kind of do this stuff because I saw it in my own household, what people can do other than what people tell them they can do, you know what I mean. And so I'm able to do that, and it's just a, it's a great thing, yeah. We see sorrows, but we also see a lot of victories.
[03:42] (Crew thanks him, 03:42–03:51.)
